headline: The week October went from 70% to 25%
standfirst: Weekend edition. On Monday futures priced a 28 October hike at more than 70%; by Thursday's close it was about 25%, and it took four sessions of one-way front-end news to get there: job openings at a five-month low and consumer confidence at a 2014 low on Tuesday, John Williams saying there was 'no need for urgency', a core PCE that printed 3.0% against 3.3% on Wednesday after the BEA rewrote July, and Vice Chair Jefferson on Thursday saying the committee may need time to see the data. The two-year fell from a 4.96% high on Tuesday to 4.79% at Thursday's close. The long end heard a different week — GDP revised to 2.2%, a 58.8 Chicago PMI, ISM prices paid at 77.9, Brent up 4.4% on Thursday, gilts at a 28-year high, Logan saying rates need to rise half a point or more — and the ten-year touched 5.344%, its highest since 2002, before closing at 5.233%. The S&P 500 fell three days to a two-week low and bounced 0.19% on Thursday to 7,666.45; it is down about 1% on the week with technology and energy the only sectors higher. The dollar index is at a 17-month high after a third weekly gain, the euro at a 16-month low on France's budget, and Tokyo core CPI printed 2.7% overnight. Payrolls at 08:30 ET today, seen near 90,000; then a week of ISM services, Fed minutes and the first coupon auctions at these yields.

bullets.title: Rates: the front end priced the Fed out of October; the long end set a 2002 high anyway
bullets.text: The sequence: Tuesday, JOLTS 7.079 million and confidence 81.9, then Williams' 'no need for urgency' — October from about 70% to 50%; Wednesday, core PCE +0.2% and 3.0% against 3.3% with July revised to 3.0%, headline 3.4% — to 35–40%; Thursday, Jefferson saying any further adjustment should follow a careful look at data trends — to about 25%, with December now the favoured date. The two-year touched 4.96% on Tuesday and closed Thursday at 4.79%, down 9.6bp on the day. The long end did the opposite until Thursday afternoon: the ten-year touched 5.3% on Wednesday and 5.344% on Thursday morning after the ISM prices index, its highest since 2002, then fell 5.9bp to close at 5.233%, its largest drop in over a month; the thirty-year touched 5.642% on Wednesday, its highest since 2002, and closed Thursday at 5.616%. Two-tens is 46bp from 32bp on Monday. Logan, after Thursday's close, said policy has been 'offsides' and rates need to rise half a point or more, with no timeline; Kashkari expects one more hike this year and one in 2027; Cook said inflation has been 'too high for too long'; Goolsbee called inflation above target 'playing with fire'; Barr said more hikes are likely. September was the ten-year's worst month since 2022 and Bloomberg's global aggregate index lost 2.4%. Abroad, gilt yields hit a 28-year high on Thursday and the Bund traded near 3.65%, its highest since 2009; France presented a 2027 budget with €54 billion of savings and a deficit target of 5% that a minority government may struggle to pass, and the euro touched $1.1237. Next week brings the first coupon supply at these levels: three-year Tuesday, ten-year Wednesday, thirty-year Thursday, with the FOMC minutes on Wednesday.

bullets.title: Data: growth firm, labour steady, the price line hot — and an inflation print that was mostly revision
bullets.text: ADP 90,000 against 70,000 with August cut to 36,000; claims 197,000 against 200,000 with the four-week average at 200,000; Challenger layoffs down 18% to 43,281 though hiring plans were the lowest September since 2011; JOLTS 7.079 million, the lowest since March, with hires up and layoffs down. Final Q2 GDP 2.2% from 1.5% with the first quarter lifted to 2.5%, consumer spending 3.8%, business investment up 9%. Chicago PMI 58.8 from 47.1, the strongest since 2022; ISM manufacturing 54.5 against 55.0, a ninth month of expansion with new orders 55.3 and backlogs 56.4, but prices paid 77.9 against 72.3 — the highest since May, back to the March level when the war began, 58.6% of respondents paying more and none paying less, ISM citing steel, aluminium, tariffs and petroleum products. Core PCE 3.0% is the number everyone will quote and the one to handle with care: the BEA's annual update revised July to 3.0% from 3.3% and headline July to 3.4% from 3.7%, so most of the gap to consensus was history rewritten; August itself was +0.2% core and +0.3% headline, soft but not a break. Income rose only 0.2% against spending +0.9%. Abroad: German CPI 3.3% against 3.1%, Italy 4.1%, Spain 5.0%; Swiss CPI 1.0% as expected; Australia 4.0% with a soft 0.2% monthly trimmed mean; China's PMIs back above 50; Japan's Tankan 24 against 25; Tokyo core CPI 2.7% against 2.4% with the core-core measure at 3.0%, its first 3-handle since August 2025.

bullets.title: Oil: a $4 Thursday on China's export halt and a third carrier group, after the November roll
bullets.text: December Brent settled $4.28 or 4.37% higher at $102.31 on Thursday and WTI $2.45 or 2.71% higher at $92.87 after Chinese refiners suspended oil-product exports beyond Hong Kong and Macau, PetroChina cancelled gasoline and jet-fuel cargoes, the Wall Street Journal reported the Pentagon may send a third aircraft-carrier strike group and 10,000 sailors and Marines to the Gulf, Iran's strait authority said several tankers had been attacked in recent days, and Trump said increased strikes were 'possible' after the midterms; Washington is also pressing Europe to draw down emergency diesel stocks. This morning Brent is near $102.1–102.8 and WTI $91.50–93.14. The week's arithmetic needs the roll: November Brent expired on Wednesday at $103.53, December traded $96.30 on Tuesday and $102.31 on Thursday, so the front-month chart shows a week down about 1.9% while the December contract rose about 6% in two days; WTI, which did not roll, is flat on the week after 5% in September and 14% for Brent. Barclays raised its fourth-quarter Brent forecast by $20 to $115 and its 2026 average to $100; BMI expects the conflict to run into early 2027; Goldman keeps $85 for year-end with Gulf exports back to their 2025 average and Kpler counting at least 16.5 million barrels a day leaving the Gulf excluding Iran in September. Refined products remain the gap: exports at roughly half of pre-war, US gasoline stocks at a 12-year low, heating oil up 116% this year. Energy was the best sector on Thursday at +1.95% and is up 40% in 2026. Gold is $4,218, down 2.4% on the week; the Bank of Korea said it will start buying in December.

bullets.title: Equities: a three-day slide, a Thursday bounce, Micron up and Nike down, Europe at a four-month low
bullets.text: The S&P 500 closed September at 7,651.54 — down 0.45% on the month, up 2.03% on the quarter, with the Dow −4.29% and −2.70% and the Nasdaq +1.86% and +2.47% — then fell to a two-week low on Thursday morning as yields spiked and recovered to close up 0.19% at 7,666.45 when they reversed; the Dow added 0.04% to 50,926.56 and the Nasdaq 0.04% to 26,871.60. The semiconductor index rose 1.59%: Micron gained 3.03% after reporting revenue of $54.23 billion, up 379%, and guiding the current quarter to $60–63 billion against $57.4 billion; Nvidia rose 1.09% to its highest since mid-May; Applied Materials 3.5%, SK Hynix 5.08%; Alphabet fell 1.7%, Broadcom 2.15%, Apple 0.81%. Accenture's revenue outlook helped technology lead. After the close Nike earned 48 cents against 44 expected on revenue of $11.21 billion against $11.32 billion, Greater China down 26%, cut its fiscal-2027 earnings guide to $1.15–1.35 against $1.67 and announced a restructuring with $2.5 billion of savings and layoffs from 2027; the shares fell 6–9% after hours, already down 44% this year. Europe had its worst day in months: the Stoxx 600 −1.30% to 626.65, its lowest since June, the FTSE 100 −1.68%, the CAC −1.62%, the FTSE MIB −2.21%, the DAX −1.03%, banks leading the falls. The VIX is 16.39, up 10% on the week. In Asia the Nikkei rose 3.24% on Thursday on Micron's read-across and gave back 0.96% this morning; the Hang Seng reopened 2.64% lower on property and tech; the Kospi is up 0.1%, the ASX 0.57%; mainland China is shut until 8 October and India today. The dollar index at 102.08 is at a 17-month high after a third weekly gain; USD/JPY slipped to 157.8 on the Tokyo CPI; Bitcoin is $86,127, up 2% on the week.

bullets.title: Today and the week ahead: payrolls, ISM services, the FOMC minutes and three auctions
bullets.text: Friday: euro-area flash HICP at 05:00 ET seen 3.6% after 3.2% with core 2.5%, the print that decides whether 29 October is an ECB hike after this week's halving of the odds; payrolls at 08:30 with consensus between 84,000 and 95,000 after 162,000, the FactSet median 90,000 in a 60,000–130,000 range, Barclays at 50,000 and expecting August revised down, unemployment 4.1%, earnings +0.3% and 3.2% on the year, private payrolls 80,000; factory orders at 10:00 seen +0.1%; Baker Hughes rigs at 13:00; the ECB's Nagel in the evening. Monday: ISM services at 10:00 ET after 55.4 with prices paid 72.6; China shut all week. Tuesday: Williams at 09:05, the three-year auction at 13:00, Lamb Weston and RPM. Wednesday: the ten-year auction at 13:00 and the FOMC minutes of the 16 September meeting at 14:00; Constellation Brands before the open, Levi Strauss after the close. Thursday: the ECB accounts at 07:30, claims at 08:30, PepsiCo before the open, the thirty-year auction at 13:00, Musalem at 13:40. Friday 9 October: Canada's jobs report at 08:30, Michigan sentiment preliminary at 10:00 after a 48.1 that was the series' low with one-year inflation expectations at 4.6%, Delta before the open. Then Columbus Day on the 12th with the bond market shut, the RBA minutes and German final HICP on the 13th with JPMorgan, Goldman, Wells Fargo and Citigroup opening the bank reporting season, China CPI, US CPI and the Beige Book on the 14th, retail sales and PPI on the 15th, China's Q3 GDP on the 16th, UK labour data on the 20th and UK CPI on the 21st, the flash PMIs on the 23rd, and the FOMC on the 27th–28th.

calendar.note: Seen 3.6% after 3.2%, core 2.5%, with Germany 3.3%, Italy 4.1% and Spain 5.0% already in. October's ECB odds halved this week to about 30% as the euro hit a 16-month low; this print decides whether they come back.

Consensus 84,000–95,000 after 162,000, unemployment 4.1%, earnings +0.3%. ADP said 90,000, claims 197,000. October's Fed hike is priced near 25%; a strong print and a 0.4% wage month put it back towards a coin flip, a weak one confirms December.
Seen +0.1% after +0.9%, with revised durable goods. Second-tier on payrolls day; the ECB's Nagel speaks in the evening.
After 55.4 and 72.6. Manufacturing prices paid jumped to 77.9 on Thursday; if services follows, the 'inflation is energy' argument gets harder. China is shut all week.
The man who started the repricing, the week after. The three-year is the first coupon auction since the ten-year touched 5.344%; the last cleared at 4.474%.

How many of the twelve wanted a faster path, and whether 'no need for urgency' was already the committee's centre on 16 September. The ten-year auction an hour earlier is the week's test of term premium; the last cleared at 4.834%.
PepsiCo before the open. The thirty-year auction comes a week after the long bond touched 5.642%, its highest since 2002; the last cleared at 5.308% and Barclays talks about 6%.

September's 48.1 was the series' low with one-year inflation expectations at 4.6%; the Conference Board's measure hit a 2014 low this week. Delta reports before the open. Columbus Day follows on Monday with the bond market shut.

sessionNote: Payrolls day, and the asymmetry matters more than the consensus. October is priced near 25% after a week in which every front-end input pointed one way; a print at 90,000 with 0.3% wages confirms what is already priced and the reaction fades, a 130,000 with a 0.4% wage month has 45 points of hike odds to recover and the two-year 17bp of room back to Tuesday's high, a 50,000 with a downward revision to August's 162,000 — Barclays' call — takes December down with October. Watch the two-year at 08:30 ET, not the headline index. The long end is a separate trade: Thursday's reversal from 5.344% was the first bond rally in a week and it came on Jefferson, not on data, so a strong number can push the ten-year back through 5.30% while the front end rallies. Brent at $102 and a third carrier group are the weekend risk; the Pentagon report landed after European markets closed and Europe reopens on it. Tokyo gave back 0.96% of Thursday's 3.24% and Hong Kong fell 2.64% on reopening; mainland China is shut until Thursday and India today, so Asian liquidity is thin into the US open. The dollar index at 102 and the euro at $1.124 have the week's trend; the yen at 157.8 has the week's one counter-trend after Tokyo's 2.7%. The brief, the map and the calendar hold until Monday's open, which means Friday's payrolls, Friday's close and anything the weekend brings are not in these pages — read them as the state of play at 06:00 UTC Friday.
watchOut: Three traps in one print. First, the headline is not the number: August's 162,000 was a seasonal-adjustment outlier by Barclays' reckoning and a large downward revision would turn a consensus September into a weak two-month run, while a 0.4% average-hourly-earnings month would matter more to the Fed than 20,000 jobs either way. Second, the reaction is asymmetric by construction: with October at 25% the market has far more room to add hike odds than to remove them, so a modest beat can move the two-year more than a modest miss, and a move that reverses within the hour was positioning, not a view. Third, the Brent columns: the front-month chart shows a week down 1.9% because the November contract expired at $103.53 on Wednesday, but the December contract that replaced it rose about 6% from Tuesday's low to Thursday's settle — anyone quoting 'oil fell this week' is reading the roll. And one for Monday: this weekend edition expires at the London open, so payrolls, the euro-area inflation print, Friday's close and whatever the carrier-group story becomes are not in it. Size for a two-way 08:30 ET, keep the oil contract straight, and treat Thursday's bond rally as one session until the auctions next week say otherwise.

archive.headline: Core PCE 3.0%. Bonds' worst month since 2022.
archive.summary: Core PCE printed 3.0% against 3.3% after the BEA's annual revision rewrote July, ADP beat at 90,000, final Q2 GDP was revised up to 2.2% and Chicago PMI jumped to 58.8; October's hike odds slid to 35–40% while the ten-year and thirty-year rose again to close a September in which the ten-year added about 50bp, its worst month since 2022. Micron beat and guided above consensus; the November Brent contract expired at $103.53; the Nikkei rose 3.24%.

archive.headline: October hike back to a coin flip.
archive.summary: Job openings fell to a five-month low, consumer confidence to a 2014 low and Williams said there was 'no need for urgency', taking October's hike from about 70% to about 50% priced; the two-year fell 6bp while the thirty-year touched 5.621%, its highest since 2002. Brent settled 2.6% lower on recovering Saudi exports, Australia's CPI printed 4.0% and the Aussie fell through 70 cents.

archive.headline: The ten-year closed at 5.24%. Nothing else mattered.
archive.summary: The ten-year closed at 5.236%, its highest since 2007, and the S&P 500 fell 0.77% to a ten-session low as Trump's rejection of Iran's Hormuz offer put Brent back above $107; Cook and Barkin talked rates higher, gold fell 3% to a seven-week low, and the RBA hiked to 4.60% overnight. The November Brent roll and Washington's reply to Tehran via Qatar were the day's traps.

archive.headline: Trump said no. Oil is back above $107.
archive.summary: Trump rejected Iran's seven-day Hormuz offer over the weekend and Brent recovered Friday's fall before New York opened; gold fell to its lowest since early August, the Kospi lost 2.5% and the dollar hit a two-month high. The front end eased with October's hike odds while the long end kept rising, into a week of PCE, ISM and payrolls.

archive.headline: The week the Treasury market stopped waiting for the Fed
archive.summary: Weekend edition. The ten-year went from 4.95% to 5.21% in a week on a 58.4 flash PMI, three auctions at two-decade highs and eight Fed speakers, and every Treasury from two years out cleared 5%. Equities held on Meta and AMD while the Dow fell for a fourth week, Brent round-tripped $100–$99–$106 on Iran, and October was 71% priced for a second hike.

archive.headline: A survey took the ten-year to 5.11%. An auction kept it there.
archive.summary: A flash composite PMI of 58.4, the highest since July 2021, took the ten-year up 14.6bp to 5.116% — its worst day since April 2025 — and a $70 billion five-year auction stopped at 5.033%, the highest since 2006. Barr said further hikes were likely needed and October went to 73% priced; every sector but energy fell and Brent rose back above $100.

archive.headline: The Fed said “we’ll see”. The two-year auction said 4.787%.
archive.summary: Treasury sold $69 billion of two-years at 4.787%, the highest stop since May 2024, on demand that held; Brent settled at $99.25 for its first close under $100 since 9 September; four Fed officials, none voting this year, all leaned toward more. The Nasdaq closed at a second straight record while financials fell 1.97%.
